title: Starship Reaches Orbit, but Its Booster Misses the Big Catch
summary:
SpaceX's giant Starship rocket soared into orbit on Friday in its boldest test yet, but the first part of its planned double catch went wrong.

The plan was to recover the whole rocket at its launch pad in Starbase, Texas. Giant mechanical arms on the launch tower were supposed to pluck the booster out of the air as it returned, then do the same for the spacecraft. No one has ever recovered a whole rocket this way.

The booster, called Super Heavy, is 236 feet tall. Shortly after liftoff, it malfunctioned. An automatic abort sent it into the Gulf of Mexico instead of back to the pad, where it exploded in the water. SpaceX had already caught three boosters before, but this was the first try with the upgraded, taller version.

The spacecraft part, 171 feet tall, kept flying. It reached orbit and prepared to deliver 26 of SpaceX's most advanced Starlink satellites. It was to circle Earth 15 times, about 170 miles up, over about 22 hours, then steer back to the pad on Saturday for its own catch attempt. Together, booster and spacecraft stand 407 feet tall, making Starship the biggest and most powerful rocket in the world.

Reusing the whole rocket could make launches cheaper and far more frequent. Elon Musk, who leads SpaceX, says that is what it will take to build moon bases and send people to Mars.

In the first full test in 2023, several engines failed to light and the self-destruct system switched on. The September test was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX tried no recovery.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land its Artemis astronauts on the moon using Starships, with a touchdown possible as early as 2028.
why_it_matters: Reusable rockets could make space travel much cheaper and more common, which matters for future trips to the moon and Mars. The test shows how hard it is to catch a giant rocket, and how much is still being learned.
